prompt:
Research what the Python Software Foundation or the CPython developers have officially said about the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build. Cite the PEP or documentation page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

If you're not sure about something, just say so.

response.content:
The Python Software Foundation and CPython developers have outlined specific performance expectations and trade-offs for the free-threaded (no-GIL) build through PEP 703, PEP 779, and official documentation. The consensus is that while the free-threaded build incurs a performance penalty in single-threaded or linear workloads due to thread-safety overheads, this cost is considered acceptable given the benefits of true parallelism on multi-core systems.

Here are the specific statements regarding performance impact:

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "The changes to make CPython thread-safe without the GIL increase execution overhead for `--disable-gil` builds." | CLAIM: The free-threaded build inherently has higher execution overhead compared to the standard GIL-enabled build.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "On the pyperformance benchmark suite, the average overhead ranges from about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux systems." | CLAIM: Official documentation quantifies the single-threaded performance overhead as varying by platform, generally staying under 10% on most systems.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "The performance penalty on linear performance, comparing a free-threaded build against a with-GIL build, as measured by the pyperformance benchmarks... is currently around 10% (except on macOS, where it’s more like 3%)." | CLAIM: Recent measurements cited in PEP 779 indicate a linear performance penalty of approximately 10% on Linux and Windows, and 3% on macOS.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "For phase II (not the default flip), we propose 15% as a hard performance target." | CLAIM: The developers have set a hard acceptance criterion of no more than 15% performance regression for the free-threaded build to be considered officially supported.

SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "At this point we’re expecting a (worst case) performance penalty of 10-15%." | CLAIM: The Steering Council explicitly acknowledged an expected worst-case performance penalty of 10-15% when accepting PEP 703.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "Realistically, though, higher memory use is the cost of having efficient, safe free-threading, and we are unlikely to get this very close to the with-GIL build’s memory use without significant performance cost." | CLAIM: Developers state that increased memory usage (currently estimated at 15-20%) is an inherent trade-off for achieving thread safety without the GIL.

SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "While not all software will benefit from this automatically, programs designed with threading in mind will run faster on multi-core hardware." | CLAIM: The performance benefit of the free-threaded build is contingent on the application's ability to utilize multiple threads effectively.
